---
title: "Understanding Swedish elections"
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

This guide explains the electoral context needed to interpret swelections data.
It is not a complete account of Swedish electoral law. The rules below describe
the current system unless a historical change is specified; use the rules for
the relevant election when comparing years. See [Coverage](coverage.html) for
available data and [Sources & methodology](sources-methodology.html) for how
they are constructed and checked.

## Electoral geography

- **Electoral constituencies** are areas used to allocate seats. The Riksdag
  has parliamentary constituencies; regional and municipal councils may also
  have several constituencies. Only some municipalities are divided this way.
- **Voting districts** are smaller geographic units for election-day voting
  and the reporting of ordinary polling-station results.
- **Polling stations** are the places where election-day voting takes place.
  Each voting district has an assigned polling station. A station is a location,
  not another result level in swelections; venue details are separate from the
  result tables described here.

The Election Authority explains these distinctions in its
[guide to constituencies and voting districts](https://www.val.se/det-svenska-valsystemet/grunderna-i-det-svenska-valsystemet/valkretsar-och-valdistrikt).

Current ordinary voting-district codes have eight digits, `LLKKXXXX`: two for
the county, two more for the municipality, and four for the district within it.
For example, `01140101` identifies county `01`, municipality `0114` and district
`0101`. Keep codes as text to preserve leading zeros. This is the current
[official coding convention](https://valcentralen.val.se/kommun/valgeografi-for-kommuner/genomfor-oversyn-av-valdistrikt),
not a guarantee that every historical source or special reporting unit uses
that format. Codes alone do not establish comparable boundaries over time.

### Collection districts

Not all votes are counted at an ordinary polling station or reported for an
ordinary voting district. Late-arriving advance votes and votes from abroad
are among those handled in **collection districts**, also called Wednesday
units in some sources. A collection district corresponds to a municipal
constituency, or to the whole municipality if it is not divided into
constituencies. This is why municipal constituency boundaries affect where
these votes can be observed. The reported votes cannot be allocated to
individual ordinary voting districts.

The preliminary count includes election-night counting and the subsequent
collection count. The final count checks the votes and counts personal votes.
The stages are distinct; `count = "preliminary"` is not simply an incomplete
version of `count = "final"`. See the Election Authority's
[description of preliminary and collection counting](https://www.val.se/det-svenska-valsystemet/rostrakning-och-mandatfordelning/preliminar-rostrakning).

`swelections` retains the reporting units supported by each source and does not
artificially distribute collection votes across ordinary districts. Historical
reporting structures differ. Historical district boundaries are not currently
harmonised across elections.

## From votes to seats

Swedish elections use proportional seat allocation: parties' shares of seats
are intended to reflect their shares of votes, subject to eligibility rules
and thresholds. In elections with several constituencies, **fixed seats** are
allocated within constituencies and **adjustment seats** help bring the overall
allocation closer to proportionality. The Riksdag uses both. Regional and
municipal councils with several constituencies also use both under current
rules. A single-constituency election, including Sweden's European Parliament
election, has no such split. See the Election Authority's
[seat-allocation guide](https://www.val.se/det-svenska-valsystemet/rostrakning-och-mandatfordelning/sa-fordelas-mandaten).

Current party thresholds are:

| Election | Threshold for participation in seat allocation |
| --- | --- |
| Riksdag | 4% nationally; alternatively, 12% in a constituency permits participation in its fixed-seat allocation only |
| European Parliament | 4% nationally |
| Regional council | 3% across the region |
| Municipal council, one constituency | 2% across the municipality |
| Municipal council, several constituencies | 3% across the municipality |

Crossing a threshold permits participation; it does not itself guarantee a seat.
The [Elections Act, chapter 14](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/vallag-2005837_sfs-2005-837/)
sets out these rules.

Explicit municipal party thresholds and municipal adjustment seats were first
applied in the **2018 ordinary elections**, following legislation that entered
into force in 2015. Earlier municipal elections had no explicit party threshold
or adjustment seats, although the number of available seats imposed a practical
barrier to small parties. Regional adjustment seats are older: they were first
used in the **1976 county-council elections**. These were not simultaneous local
and regional reforms. See the official
[2018 election report](https://www.val.se/download/18.162047b519a91d0533117a82/1592299588277/erfarenhetsrapport-2018.pdf)
and [historical account in SOU 2012:94](https://data.riksdagen.se/dokument/H0B394).

`seats()` reports the established allocations, rather than recalculating all
elections under today's rules.

## How candidates are elected

First, seats are allocated to parties. Personal votes can then affect which
of a party's candidates receive those seats. Candidates reaching the personal
vote threshold are considered first, ordered by their personal votes. Remaining
places are determined from the candidate order on the ballot lists and the
applicable counting rules. Multiple lists and candidates elected in more than
one constituency require further rules; ballot position alone is not always
enough to reconstruct the outcome.

Currently, the personal-vote threshold is 5% of the party's votes in the
constituency, with additional minima of 100 personal votes in regional elections
and 50 in municipal elections. For the European Parliament, the threshold is
5% of the party's votes nationally. Reaching the threshold does not create an
additional party seat. See the Election Authority's
[guide to choosing elected members](https://www.val.se/det-svenska-valsystemet/rostrakning-och-mandatfordelning/sa-utses-ledamoter).

In the package, `seats()` describes party allocations, `preference_votes()`
describes reported personal votes, `candidates()` summarises candidate records,
and `elected()` identifies the reported elected candidates. Subsequent mandate
holding is a separate question, covered by the mandate-period functions.

## Personal votes and candidate nomination

The modern personal-voting system was tried in **seven municipalities in 1994**
and used in Sweden's **1995 European Parliament election** before its broad
introduction in the **1998 Riksdag, county-council and municipal elections**.
See the official [review of the first decade of personal voting](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/statens-offentliga-utredningar/ett-decennium-med-personval-erfarenheter-och_gvb368/html/).
The Riksdag personal-vote threshold was originally 8%; the reduction to 5% was
first applied in the **2014 election**, as recorded in the
[constitutional committee's review](https://data.riksdagen.se/fil/B8A1A05A-B7A3-4DC2-A962-561BAEDDAAE3).
Personal-vote rules have therefore changed within the package's coverage.

Nomination rules also changed gradually. Sweden historically allowed voters
broad freedom to nominate candidates by adding names to ballots. From the
1998 elections, parties could protect their nominations by registering their
party designation and notifying all their candidates, with their consent;
other parties remained subject to broader voter nomination. See
[SOU 2012:94](https://data.riksdagen.se/dokument/H0B394).
The later reform requiring advance party participation and candidate consent
was first applied at the 2018 ordinary elections. Open and locked candidate
lists still differ under current rules; open lists do not dispense with the
consent requirement. See the
[Elections Act and its transitional provisions](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/vallag-2005837_sfs-2005-837/)
and the official [2026 review of the ballot system](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/statens-offentliga-utredningar/710-miljoner-skal-till-reformer_heb32/html/).

Older candidate records therefore need not describe exactly the same nominated
population as later files. `candidacies()` preserves election-specific candidacies
and list positions; `candidates()` provides candidate summaries within the
relevant election and party. Neither names nor candidate numbers establish
physical-person identity across elections.

## Historical comparability

Three kinds of change matter for comparisons over time:

- **Electoral rules:** personal voting, party thresholds and adjustment seats.
- **Electoral geography:** constituency and voting-district boundaries.
- **Administrative geography:** municipalities, counties and other units,
  including changes in their boundaries and codes.

`swelections` preserves the historical units reported by its sources; it does
not treat equal codes or names as proof of unchanged geography. Better
comparability over time, including harmonisation of historical geographies,
is a long-term development goal, not an existing feature. See
[Sources & methodology](sources-methodology.html) for source handling and
[Coverage](coverage.html) for available levels and limitations.
